subject: Government
title: Political Culture and Socialization
outline: Meaning and importance of political socialization

modules.title: Political Culture
modules.html:
Political culture is the pattern of beliefs, attitudes, values, sentiments and orientations that a people hold towards their political system and their own role within it. It is, in short, the political personality of a society. The concept was popularised by Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba in The Civic Culture (1963).

TypeOrientation of citizensTypical setting
ParochialLittle or no awareness of the national political system; loyalty to clan or village.Remote traditional communities.
SubjectAware of government and its output, but passive – they obey rather than participate.Authoritarian or military regimes.
ParticipantAware, informed and actively involved in inputs (voting, party work, protest).Mature democracies.

Almond and Verba argued that stable democracy rests on a civic culture, a balanced mixture of all three in which participation is tempered by deference and trust. Political culture may also be described as dominant (shared by the majority) or a sub-culture (held by an ethnic, regional or religious minority). Where sub-cultures conflict sharply, the culture is called fragmented; Nigeria's ethnic and religious cleavages illustrate this.

examples.q: A villager who has never heard of the National Assembly exhibits which political culture?
examples.a: A parochial political culture – there is no awareness of, or orientation towards, the national political system.

modules.title: Political Socialization and Its Agents
modules.html:
Political socialization is the lifelong process by which individuals acquire their political values, attitudes and patterns of behaviour. It transmits political culture from one generation to the next.

Agents of political socialization:

  • The family — the earliest and most enduring agent; children absorb party loyalties and attitudes to authority.
  • The school — civic education, debating societies, prefect elections, the national anthem and pledge.
  • Peer groups — friends and age-grades shape opinions, especially in adolescence.
  • Religious institutions — churches and mosques preach values of obedience, justice and communal duty.
  • The mass media — newspapers, radio, television and now social media set the agenda of public debate.
  • Political parties and pressure groups — rallies, manifestos and campaigns.
  • Government agencies — NYSC, National Orientation Agency, INEC voter education.
  • The workplace and trade unions.

Importance: it produces loyal and informed citizens, promotes national integration, stabilises the political system, recruits future leaders, and legitimises the regime.

examples.q: Name two government agencies used for political socialization in Nigeria and state their contribution.
examples.a: The National Youth Service Corps posts graduates outside their state of origin to promote national unity; the National Orientation Agency runs campaigns on civic responsibility and values.

modules.title: Political Participation and Political Apathy
modules.html:
Political participation covers all voluntary activities by which citizens influence the selection of rulers and the making of policy. Ranked from least to most demanding: discussing politics, voting, attending rallies, joining a party, campaigning, contributing funds, contesting elections, holding office.

Political apathy is a lack of interest or indifference to political activity. Causes include:

  • Illiteracy and ignorance of political processes.
  • Electoral malpractice, rigging and violence, which convince voters that their vote does not count.
  • Poverty and preoccupation with survival.
  • Broken promises and corruption — loss of confidence in politicians.
  • Long distances to polling units and cumbersome registration.
  • Fear of victimisation; religious or cultural restrictions.

Remedies: mass civic education, free and fair elections, use of technology such as BVAS to protect the vote, decent polling arrangements, punishment of electoral offenders, and responsive government that visibly delivers services.

examples.q: Suggest two practical measures to reduce voter apathy in Nigeria.
examples.a: (i) Sustained voter education by INEC and the National Orientation Agency, especially in rural areas. (ii) Credible, transparent elections with results transmitted electronically so citizens see that their votes count.

modules.title: Political Culture in Nigeria
modules.html:
Nigeria's political culture is best described as fragmented and transitional. Its main features are:

  • Ethnicity and regionalism — voters often support candidates from their own group, producing a politics of identity rather than of issues.
  • Godfatherism and patron–client politics — sponsorship of candidates in exchange for patronage.
  • Religion as a strong political marker, especially along the northern–southern divide.
  • The prebendal use of office — public office treated as an opportunity for private gain.
  • Militarised attitudes inherited from long years of military rule: intolerance of opposition, command style.
  • Growing civic assertiveness among urban youth, expressed through social media and mass protests.

Nation-building instruments — the federal character principle, NYSC, unity schools, quota admissions and a national language policy — are deliberate attempts to build a common participant culture out of these fragments.

examples.q: Why is Nigeria's political culture called 'transitional'?
examples.a: Because it is moving from largely parochial and subject orientations, reinforced by decades of military rule, towards a participant culture, without having fully arrived; elements of all three co-exist.
